articles.title: Stony Brook professor honored with innovation award bearing her name
articles.description: By Michael Ganci Esther Sans Takeuchi had just finished one of the biggest talks of her career when she was asked not to leave the stage. The Stony Brook University distinguished professor had delivered the plenary address at the Electrochemical Society’s 250th meeting in Calgary, Canada. When she finished, the society’s chief executive asked her to stay at the podium. “He said, ‘We have a surprise for you,’” Takeuchi said. “They had done a good job keeping a secret because I had no idea.” The surprise was the Esther Sans Takeuchi Innovation Award, a new honor that will recognize people who have made substantial and sustained impacts on electrochemistry, particularly through technologies used in energy and the environment. Nominations for the first award open March 15, 2027. “I’ve been privileged to receive awards, but what’s special about this award is that it’s named after me and leaves a legacy,” Takeuchi said. “Years and years from now, people will still be receiving an award in my name.” Takeuchi holds the William and Jane Knapp Chair in Energy and the Environment at Stony Brook University, where she has worked since 2012 after leaving the University at Buffalo. She also serves as chief scientist at Brookhaven National Laboratory and was president of the ECS from 2011 to 2012. A picket fence of patents Takeuchi holds more than 150 patents and has been inducted into the National Inventors Hall of Fame. In 2008, she received the National Medal of Technology and Innovation for her work on the battery that powers implantable cardiac defibrillators. That work began at her first job out of school, at Wilson Greatbatch Ltd. in Clarence, just outside Buffalo. At the time it was a small, family-owned company building batteries for implantable medical devices while competing against billion-dollar device makers that produced their own. The strategy that helped the small team keep up came from her husband, Kenneth Takeuchi. “He said you should patent not only what you think you’re going to use in the product, but put up what’s called a picket fence,” she said. That meant patenting the ideas surrounding an invention too, including ones a competitor might use to design around it. As device makers asked for batteries that were smaller and lasted longer, Takeuchi and her team kept reinventing the design. “With the pace of technology change, it’s a rare thing to have an invention be on the market for decades,” she said. “But this battery is still used in medical devices today. It’s still improving the quality of life and saving lives.” A lesson from Latvia Takeuchi said much of who she is comes from her parents, who fled their homeland during World War II. Both were college educated in Latvia, in northeastern Europe. Her father was an electrical engineer, and her mother had a degree in economics. When their country was overrun during the war, they left with Takeuchi’s sister, who was about 3 years old, and little more than a couple of suitcases. The family ended up in displaced persons camps in Germany, where Takeuchi’s brother was born. In the early 1950s, a church congregation sponsored them, and they moved to Kansas City, Missouri, where Takeuchi was born. When she was about 4, the family moved to Akron, Ohio, after her father got a job as an electrical engineer at Goodyear Aerospace. “They thought they would always go back, and they never did,” she said. “They never could.” “He said you can’t predict circumstances in your life, but if you have an education, that’s something that no one can take away from you,” Takeuchi said of her father. She and both of her siblings earned doctorates. Takeuchi received her bachelor’s degree from the University of Pennsylvania and her doctorate in chemistry from Ohio State University. Passing it on At Stony Brook, Takeuchi, her husband and longtime collaborator Amy Marschilok co-advise 16 doctoral candidates through the university’s Institute of Sustainability, Electrification and Energy, which Takeuchi co-directs. Marschilok has worked alongside Takeuchi since about 2007, following her from Greatbatch, Texas, to Buffalo. “The students are motivated by the opportunity to make a difference and to make the world a better place,” Takeuchi said. “That’s a real privilege, to have a job where we can be motivated and motivate others to do good.” Her advice for young inventors is to be fearless, but also to know their field. “You can have an idea, but you need to know that your idea is new,” she said. Takeuchi and her husband have been married 44 years, and she is quick to share the credit with him. “I’ve received a lot of the accolades, but the truth is he deserves the accolades as much or more than I do,” she said.
